ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: Given: As shown in the diagram, in $\triangle ABC$, $\angle ACB = 90^\circ$, and $BC = BD$, $AC = AE$, then what is the degree measure of $\angle DCE$?
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text:
\textbf{Solution:} Given that AC=AE and BC=BD,\\
let $\angle$AEC=$\angle$ACE=x and $\angle$BDC=$\angle$BCD=y,\\
then $\angle$A=180$^\circ$-2x and $\angle$B=180$^\circ$-2y,\\
since $\angle$ACB+$\angle$A+$\angle$B=$180^\circ$,\\
thus 90$^\circ$+(180$^\circ$-2x)+(180$^\circ$-2y)=180$^\circ$,\\
hence x+y=135$^\circ$,\\
therefore, $\angle$DCE=180$^\circ$-($\angle$AEC+$\angle$BDC)=180$^\circ$-(x+y)=\boxed{45^\circ}.

method.method_draft: First describe the diagram: A, D, E, B are collinear with D and E between A and B, and C connects to all four points. From the text, ∠ACB is a right angle, AC = AE, and BC = BD. Use coordinates with C as the origin, ray CA as the positive x-axis and ray CB as the positive y-axis. Let AC = a, BC = b, so A = (a,0), B = (0,b), and AB = L = sqrt(a^2+b^2). Since E lies on AB with AE = a, E = A + (a/L)(B−A). Since D lies on AB with BD = b, D = B + (b/L)(A−B). Put p = a/L and q = b/L, so p^2+q^2=1. Then vectors CD and CE are proportional to (pq, q(1−q)) and (p(1−p), pq). Compute the dot product formula for the angle between CD and CE: cos∠DCE = (CD·CE)/(|CD||CE|). Simplifying with p^2+q^2=1 gives cos∠DCE = sqrt(2)/2, hence ∠DCE = 45°.

Point C is above the line, and segments CA, CD, CE, and CB are drawn, forming triangle ABC with interior segments from C to D and C to E. From the problem text, ∠ACB = 90°, AC = AE, and BC = BD.

Reasoning: Since AC = AE, triangle ACE is isosceles, so let ∠AEC = ∠ACE = x. Since BC = BD, triangle BCD is isosceles, so let ∠BDC = ∠BCD = y. Because A, D, E, B are collinear, AE lies along AB, so the angle at A of triangle ACE equals ∠CAB. Thus ∠A = 180° − 2x. Similarly, BD lies along BA, so the angle at B of triangle BCD equals ∠CBA, giving ∠B = 180° − 2y. In triangle ABC, ∠ACB = 90°, so ∠A + ∠B = 90°. Therefore (180° − 2x) + (180° − 2y) = 90°, which gives x + y = 135°. In triangle CDE, ∠CED = x because ED is along EA, and ∠CDE = y because DE is along DB. Hence ∠DCE = 180° − x − y = 180° − 135° = 45°.

ready3_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: Given: As shown in the diagram, in $\triangle ABC$, $\angle ACB = 90^\circ$, and $BC = BD$, $AC = AE$, then what is the degree measure of $\angle DCE$?
ready3_open_rewrite.raw_answer:
\textbf{Solution:} Given that $AC=AE$ and $BC=BD$,\\
let $\angle AEC=\angle ACE=x$ and $\angle BDC=\angle BCD=y$,\\
then $\angle A=180^\circ-2x$ and $\angle B=180^\circ-2y$,\\
since $\angle ACB+\angle A+\angle B=180^\circ$,\\
thus $90^\circ+(180^\circ-2x)+(180^\circ-2y)=180^\circ$,\\
hence $x+y=135^\circ$,\\
therefore, $\angle DCE=180^\circ-(\angle AEC+\angle BDC)=180^\circ-(x+y)=\boxed{45^\circ}$.
